title: the Ashtavakra Gita complete
hook: in chapter two the student stops asking and starts exclaiming, and the king bows to himself
carry: the waves that turned out to be water

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ashtavakra Gita and its line on freedom: free if you take yourself as free, bound if you take yourself as bound: the binding lives in the taking. This week ran from the Vivekachudamani's bee, rope and arrow into the Ashtavakra Gita. Did you catch anyone insisting on being stuck? Day one thousand one.
screen: `THE ASHTAVAKRA GITA.` · `THE BINDING LIVES IN THE TAKING.`

segments.voice: Aho. It's a Sanskrit cry of wonder, the sound someone makes when a thing turns out to be bigger than expected. And it's how King Janaka opens the second chapter. In the first chapter he asked his three questions and listened. Now the teacher falls silent and the student speaks, and he doesn't ask anything at all. He exclaims. A few verses in, what comes out of his mouth is surprising enough to make a first-time reader look twice. He bows to himself.
screen: `AHO: A CRY OF WONDER.` → `THE STUDENT STOPS ASKING.` → `THE KING BOWS TO HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: Here's how chapter two begins, in paraphrase. Aho, I am spotless, at peace, pure awareness, beyond nature. All this time I've been fooled by delusion. Then Janaka reaches for the sea. As waves and foam and bubbles are nothing other than water, he says, so this whole world, flowing out of the Self, is nothing other than the Self. A wave can rise high or crash on the rocks, and it never stops being water. Then come the verses that make people sit up. Wonderful am I, Janaka says. Salutation to me. Namo mahyam. I remain, he says, even when the whole world, from the creator down to a blade of grass, is destroyed. On the surface that sounds like a king who has had too much praise. But the I in these verses isn't the king. It isn't Janaka with a crown and a treasury. It's the awareness he was pointed to on the first day, the witness. When he bows to that, he's bowing to what he takes to be in everything, including the blade of grass. The line between the two is fine, and the text walks it. On this reading, the small I that wants credit is exactly what has dropped away. What's left can't be flattered, because there's no one left to flatter. That's why the chapter sounds like joy and not like vanity. A man who thought he was a wave has just found out he's water. And what he does with the discovery is not explain it. He sings.
screen: `SPOTLESS, AT PEACE, PURE AWARENESS.` · `WAVES, FOAM AND BUBBLES ARE WATER.` · `NAMO MAHYAM: SALUTATION TO ME.` · `NOT THE KING. THE WITNESS.` · then, large: `THE WAVE FINDS IT'S WATER.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Notice the thoughts and feelings rising and falling like waves: a plan, a memory, a flicker of worry. Don't try to calm them. Just watch each one rise, and watch it sink back. Then notice what they rise in, the awareness itself, the water under the waves. If a wave seems big, let it be big. It's still water. The bell holds the time.
Aho. A Sanskrit cry of wonder. Janaka opens chapter two with it, after finding out that a wave he thought he was has always been water.
Your line: the waves that turned out to be water. Today, when a strong mood rises, name it a wave once, out loud or under your breath, and watch it come back down. Day one thousand one.

howItsDone: In the Ashtavakra Gita, chapter two is Janaka's response, and students reading the text with a teacher often treat it as a picture of what the sage's teaching sounds like once it lands: wonder rather than argument.

fork.setup: you're Janaka. the sage has pointed you to awareness, and it has landed. what do you do?
options: break into wonder, and bow to the Self.
go back to running the kingdom as before.
fork.reveal: chapter two is Janaka's cry: aho, and namo mahyam, salutation to me, meaning the Self in everything.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: aho, a cry of wonder or surprise. Janaka opens chapter two with it.

trapdoor: what you thought: a king saying I am wonderful sounds like vanity.
what it means: the I he praises is awareness, the Self in everything, not the king with the crown.
what a scholar hears: verses 2.11 to 2.14 each open aho aham namo mahyam, wonderful am I, bow to me: a form of greeting turned on the Self.
